note: Group-level overview of CITES-listed fauna and non-timber flora. Not the full checklist - confirm every species on Species+.

fauna.name: Felidae
fauna.summary: The whole cat family is listed. The big cats and several others are in Appendix I (tiger, snow leopard, leopard, jaguar, cheetah, clouded leopard, Asian lion). Most other wild cats, including the African lion and the lynxes, are in Appendix II; a few populations are in Appendix III. The domestic cat is not covered.
checks: Appendix I cats: commercial trade is prohibited, so a normal trade export permit is a red flag
Leopard, cheetah and some other cats have export quotas, check the quota and tag on the skin
Big-cat bones and derivatives are often declared as other animals or as medicine

fauna.name: Elephantidae
fauna.summary: Asian elephants are in Appendix I. African elephants are in Appendix I, except the populations of Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe, which are in Appendix II under a special annotation with strict conditions on trade in ivory.
products: raw and worked ivory (tusks, carvings, jewellery)
checks: Commercial international trade in ivory is not allowed
Pre-Convention (antique) ivory needs a pre-Convention certificate and proof of date, many countries also restrict domestic sale
Ivory is frequently hidden in containers under other goods, compare the declared goods with X-ray images

fauna.name: Rhinocerotidae
fauna.summary: All rhinoceroses are in Appendix I. The only exception is the southern white rhino (Ceratotherium simum simum) of South Africa and Eswatini, in Appendix II for live animals and hunting trophies only; everything else is treated as Appendix I.
checks: Rhino horn trade is among the most heavily trafficked, treat any horn shipment as suspect without full documents
Trophy export needs the correct purpose code and permits for each specimen

fauna.name: Primates
fauna.summary: All primates are listed. The apes (gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos, orangutans, gibbons), many lemurs and many monkeys are in Appendix I; the rest, including most macaques, baboons and marmosets, are in Appendix II.
checks: Live primates need documentation of legal origin and humane transport
Captive-bred claims (source C) on Appendix I primates need checking against the breeder's registration

fauna.name: Pangolins (Manidae)
fauna.summary: All eight pangolin species are in Appendix I (since 2017). Pangolins are among the most trafficked mammals in the world.
checks: Scales are often declared as other goods or hidden among legal cargo
Any pangolin consignment needs the full Appendix I document set

fauna.name: Ursidae
fauna.summary: All bears are listed. The giant panda and several Asian bears (sun bear, sloth bear, Asiatic black bear) are in Appendix I, as are some brown bear populations. The polar bear, American black bear and the remaining brown bear populations are in Appendix II.
checks: Bile and gall bladders show up inside traditional medicine products, check ingredients and annotations

fauna.name: Cetacea
fauna.summary: All whales, dolphins and porpoises are listed. The great whales and several small cetaceans are in Appendix I; the remaining species, including most dolphins, are in Appendix II. Marine specimens taken outside national waters need an introduction-from-the-sea certificate.
products: live dolphins and orcas for aquaria
checks: Live cetacean transfers need permits for each animal and recipient suitability confirmed

fauna.name: Saiga and Tibetan antelope
fauna.summary: The Tibetan antelope or chiru (Pantholops hodgsonii) is in Appendix I; its wool is sold as shahtoosh, and shahtoosh shawls are illegal to trade. Saiga antelopes (Saiga spp.) are in Appendix II, with horn used in traditional medicine.
checks: Shawls labelled as cashmere or pashmina can contain shahtoosh, laboratory confirmation is needed

fauna.name: Psittaciformes
fauna.summary: All parrots are listed in Appendix II, except those in Appendix I (for example the African grey parrot, hyacinth macaw and many cockatoos and macaws). Not covered: budgerigar, cockatiel, rose-ringed parakeet and peach-faced lovebird.
checks: Wild-caught birds are often declared as captive-bred (source C), compare with ring and breeder records
Eggs are smuggled in specially prepared containers or clothing

fauna.name: Falconiformes (raptors)
fauna.summary: Falcons, hawks, eagles, vultures and the osprey are listed. Most are in Appendix II, with several species (for example the peregrine falcon and several eagles) in Appendix I. Falconry birds crossing borders need documents for each bird.
checks: Falconry movements often involve repeated crossings, check each document applies to that bird (ring or microchip number)

fauna.name: Strigiformes (owls)
fauna.summary: Owls are listed in Appendix II, with a few species in Appendix I.
checks: Check species on mounted birds or feather products, many look-alikes exist

fauna.name: Trochilidae (hummingbirds)
fauna.summary: All hummingbirds are in Appendix II, with a few species in Appendix I.
checks: Feathers and dried skins are used for craft and jewellery, check declared species

fauna.name: Sea turtles (Cheloniidae, Dermochelyidae)
fauna.summary: All seven sea turtle species are in Appendix I.
checks: Worked tortoiseshell can look like plastic or horn, use specialist identification

fauna.name: Testudines (tortoises and freshwater turtles)
fauna.summary: All tortoises (Testudinidae) are listed, mostly in Appendix II, with several species (for example the radiated tortoise, ploughshare tortoise and Indian star tortoise) in Appendix I. Many Asian freshwater turtles are listed in Appendix II, some in Appendix I. Many species are heavily collected for the pet trade.
checks: Live turtles are often shipped in suitcases or parcels, check species with an expert

fauna.name: Crocodylia
fauna.summary: All crocodilians are listed. Most are in Appendix II, with many species and populations (for example the Chinese alligator and gharial) in Appendix I. Skins and leather goods are traded under a universal tagging system for skins.
checks: Skins must carry the tags required by the tagging system, compare the tag to the permit

fauna.name: Pythonidae
fauna.summary: All pythons are in Appendix II, except the Indian python (Python molurus molurus), which is in Appendix I.
checks: Snake leather can be difficult to identify, laboratory identification is often needed

fauna.name: Boidae (boas)
fauna.summary: Boas are listed, mostly in Appendix II, with some species and populations in Appendix I.
checks: Check species on live shipments, many boas look alike

fauna.name: Varanus (monitor lizards)
fauna.summary: Monitor lizards are listed, mostly in Appendix II, with a few species (for example the Komodo dragon) in Appendix I.
checks: Monitor skins are widely used for leather, check species and tags

fauna.name: Poison frogs and mantellas
fauna.summary: Poison dart frogs (Dendrobatidae) and mantella frogs (Mantella spp.) are listed in Appendix II, with a few species in Appendix I.
checks: Frogs are shipped in small containers, check species and documents carefully

fauna.name: Acipenseriformes (sturgeons)
fauna.summary: All sturgeons and paddlefish are in Appendix II, except a few in Appendix I (for example the European sturgeon, Acipenser sturio). Caviar and other products are covered. Caviar is traded under a universal labelling system.
checks: Caviar tins and jars must carry the non-reusable CITES label with species, source and permit information
A small quantity for personal use (commonly 125 g per person) may be exempt, check national rules

fauna.name: Hippocampus (seahorses)
fauna.summary: All seahorses (Hippocampus) are in Appendix II. Seahorses are mostly traded dried for traditional medicine, and live for aquaria.
checks: Dried seahorses are often shipped in large volumes under generic descriptions

fauna.name: Sharks and rays (selected families)
fauna.summary: Many sharks and rays are listed in Appendix II (including whale shark, great white, basking shark, hammerheads, thresher, porbeagle, oceanic whitetip, manta and devil rays, and further families listed at recent meetings). Sawfishes are in Appendix I. Fins, meat and gill plates are covered. Specimens taken from the sea outside national waters need an introduction-from-the-sea certificate.
checks: Processed fins are hard to identify, species-level testing (DNA) is usually required
Check which species and families are listed on Species+, recent meetings added many

fauna.name: Anguilla anguilla (European eel)
fauna.summary: The European eel (Anguilla anguilla) is in Appendix II. Glass eels (juveniles) are smuggled in very large numbers, usually in water-filled bags in air cargo. The EU applies strict controls and bans exports.
checks: Glass eels from other eel species can look identical, species identification is important
Declared as other fish or aquarium animals in many cases

fauna.name: Totoaba macdonaldi
fauna.summary: The totoaba (Totoaba macdonaldi), a fish of the Gulf of California, is in Appendix I. Its dried swim bladders are trafficked to Asia, and the illegal fishing kills the critically endangered vaquita porpoise.
checks: Swim bladders are often declared as other fish maw, species testing is needed

fauna.name: Corals, giant clams and queen conch
fauna.summary: All stony (hard) corals (Scleractinia), black corals, blue coral, organ pipe coral, fire corals, giant clams (Tridacnidae) and the queen conch (Strombus gigas) are in Appendix II. Fossil corals are not covered.
checks: Live coral and coral rock are traded in large volumes, check species, quantity and origin on each document

fauna.name: Birdwing and other protected butterflies
fauna.summary: Birdwing butterflies (Ornithoptera, Troides, Trogonoptera) are in Appendix II, a few species (for example Queen Alexandra's birdwing) in Appendix I. The Apollo butterfly (Parnassius apollo) is in Appendix II. Mounted and framed specimens are covered.
checks: Framed specimens are sold as souvenirs, check species and origin

fauna.name: Brachypelma (red-knee tarantulas)
fauna.summary: All Brachypelma tarantulas (for example Mexican red-knee tarantulas) are in Appendix II.
checks: Spiders are shipped in small containers, often in parcels or postal mail

flora.name: Orchidaceae
flora.summary: All orchids are listed in Appendix II. Slipper orchids (Paphiopedilum, Phragmipedium) and a few other species are in Appendix I. Seedlings or tissue cultures in vitro (in flasks) and certain artificially propagated hybrids are exempt under the annotation, check the exact text on Species+.
checks: Plants declared as artificially propagated (source A) but showing signs of wild collection (old, large, damaged, uneven sizes) are a red flag
A phytosanitary certificate is a separate document, it does not replace CITES

flora.name: Cactaceae
flora.summary: All cacti are listed in Appendix II (except Pereskia and a few others, check the annotation), and a number of genera or species (for example Ariocarpus, Obregonia, Pelecyphora, Turbinicarpus, Uebelmannia) are in Appendix I. Seeds, fruits, and cut stems or segments are not covered under certain conditions, see the annotation.
checks: Large wild-collected cacti are sometimes declared as nursery-grown, check size, age and root condition
Many rare cacti are sold online and shipped by post

flora.name: Cycadales (cycads)
flora.summary: All cycads are listed. Most are in Appendix II, and Encephalartos (all species), Cycas beddomei and a few others are in Appendix I. Cycads are slow-growing and heavily collected from the wild.
checks: Large wild-collected cycads are sometimes declared as nursery-grown (source A), check the roots and age of the plant

flora.name: Cyclamen
flora.summary: All cyclamens (Cyclamen) are in Appendix II. Artificially propagated pot cyclamen (Cyclamen persicum) are exempt under the annotation (check the text on Species+); wild-collected tubers are commonly traded.
checks: Wild-collected tubers from Turkey and neighbouring countries have been traded in large numbers

flora.name: Galanthus (snowdrops)
flora.summary: All snowdrops (Galanthus) are in Appendix II. Wild-collected bulbs are traded in large numbers from Turkey and Georgia.
checks: Bulbs are often sold in bulk by weight, check the origin and any quota on the export permit

flora.name: Cyatheaceae and Dicksoniaceae (tree ferns)
flora.summary: Tree ferns (Cyatheaceae) are listed in Appendix II, and Dicksonia sellowiana is in Appendix I. Trunks and fibre are traded for horticulture.
checks: Trunks may be declared as wood or fibre, check the species and any annotation

flora.name: Aloe
flora.summary: Aloes (Aloe) are listed in Appendix II, except Aloe vera (not listed), and a few species (for example Aloe pillansii and Aloe polyphylla) are in Appendix I. Aloe extracts and products are covered under the annotation.
checks: Aloe ferox (Cape aloe) extracts are traded with export permits, check quantities

flora.name: Euphorbia (succulent species)
flora.summary: Succulent Euphorbia species are listed in Appendix II, and a few (mostly from Madagascar) are in Appendix I. Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) and certain widely grown cultivars are not covered. Check the annotation for the exact exemptions.
checks: Many species look alike, ask for species-level identification of live plants

flora.name: Pachypodium
flora.summary: Pachypodium plants are listed in Appendix II, with a few species (for example Pachypodium ambongense, P. baronii and P. decaryi) in Appendix I.
checks: Wild-collected caudex plants can be sold as nursery plants, check size and condition

flora.name: Carnivorous plants (Nepenthes, Sarracenia)
flora.summary: Tropical pitcher plants (Nepenthes) and North American pitcher plants (Sarracenia) are listed in Appendix II, with a few species in Appendix I (for example Nepenthes rajah and N. khasiana).
checks: Check whether hybrids are covered under the annotation of the parent species

flora.name: Medicinal and aromatic plants (ginseng and others)
flora.summary: A number of medicinal and aromatic plants are in Appendix II, for example American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius), goldenseal (Hydrastis canadensis), devil's claw (Harpagophytum), Hoodia, snakeroot (Rauvolfia serpentina), spikenard (Nardostachys grandiflora) and Himalayan may apple (Podophyllum hexandrum). The annotation decides which parts and products (roots, powder, extracts, finished products) are covered.
checks: Herbal products are often declared by their trade name, check the ingredients against the annotation
Wild-harvested roots are traded with quotas set by the exporting country
